summary: Kyoko Fujii, working in Buddhist studies and Indology, studied at the University of Tokyo (~1968–1977). She served as a professor at Hokkaido University (~1997–2013) and has held roles at ICPBS, Eastern Institute, and the International Institute for Buddhist Studies.

Specializing in Buddhist studies and Sinology, Kyoko Tokuno taught Douglas Ober and held academic posts at the University of Oregon and the University of Washington, where she was attested as a professor in 2017.

Kyokuga Saeki was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who studied under numerous traditional teachers, including Gen'yū, Ryoga, and Kasho Noyama. He served as the 143rd elder at Sennyu-ji (~1888–1891) and taught Shundo Sugihara and Etō Sebe.

Kyosho Hayashima worked in Buddhist studies and Indology. He held positions at Toyo University (attested 1962), Yokohama City University (attested 1962), and the University of Tokyo (attested 1980), and taught Shinjō Kawasaki and Fumihiko Sueki.
Kyosho Tanaka is a scholar of Buddhist studies who studied at the University of Tokyo. He served as an associate professor at Musashino University, attested between 1976 and 1989.
Kyoshun Todo is a scholar of Buddhist studies who served at Bukkyo University as an assistant professor (attested 1962) and later as a professor (attested 1988–1992).

Kyotaro Nishikawa was a scholar in Buddhist studies and history and archaeology. Educated at Keio University, he served as Director-General of the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties from approximately 1990 to 1996.

Kyozan Joshu Sasaki worked in Buddhist and religious studies, studying at Zuilyo-ji and under Joten Soko Miura. He served as abbot of Yotoku-in (1948–1953) and Shojuan (1953), and founded Mount Baldy Zen Center, serving as abbot (~1971–2012).

Kyozo Yamada worked in Buddhist and religious studies, studying at the University of Tokyo and under several teachers, including Hakuun Yasutani. He founded Kamakura Haku-un-kai in 1953 and became the second head of Sanbo Kyodan in 1970.

Kyōko Fujii works in Buddhist studies and Indology. In posts attested in 2026, she served as faculty at the International College for Postgraduate Buddhist Studies and as a professor at the International Institute for Buddhist Studies.
Kōdō Kawamura was a Buddhist studies scholar who completed his master's and doctoral degrees at Komazawa University. He later held a post as a professor at Komazawa University, attested in 1994.

Kōgi Kudara was a scholar of Buddhist studies, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He served as a professor at Ryukoku University (attested 1979) and held an editorial post at the Ryukoku Buddhist Studies Association (attested 2002).

Kōjirō Yoshikawa was a Sinologist who studied at Kyoto University (~1923–1926). He served as Professor of Chinese Language and Literature at Kyoto University (~1947–1967) and as board chairman of Toho Gakkai (~1972–1980).

Kōken Unno, a scholar of Indology, Buddhist studies, and philosophy, earned master's and doctoral degrees at Nagoya University. He held positions at Nagoya University, Aichi Prefectural University of Fine Arts and Music, and Meijo University (attested 2002).

Kōshō Kawamura, working in Buddhist studies and Indology, studied at Toyo University. He held positions at Toyo University (attested 1963–1984), Hamamatsu University, Minobusan University, and served as an honorary professor at Nava Nalanda Mahavihara (attested 2001).

Kōshō Uchiyama studied Western philosophy at Waseda University and trained under Kodo Sawaki. A scholar in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and religious studies, he taught at Miyazaki Catholic Seminary and served as abbot of Antai-ji from 1965 to 1975.
Kōshō Ōtani was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the First Higher School (~1929–1932) and Tokyo Imperial University (~1932–1935). He succeeded Kozui Otani.

Lajos Ligeti studied at Eötvös Loránd University, Eötvös József Collegium, and the University of Paris under scholars including Paul Pelliot. Working in Sinology, Tibetology, and Inner Asian studies, he held the chair of Inner Asian Studies at Eötvös Loránd University.

Lakshmi Swaminathan was a scholar in Indology and linguistics. She studied at Queen Mary's College (~1930–1932) and Madras Medical College (~1932–1938), and later became a retired lecturer at Stony Brook University.

Lal Mani Joshi studied at Allahabad, BHU, and Gorakhpur under G. C. Pande. Active in Buddhist studies, Indology, and religious studies, he held posts at Gorakhpur, Punjabi University, Harvard, Amherst, Haverford, and the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies.
